heading: Step 5: Test the service and the controller
body:
A test unit is a class in `client/tests` or `server/tests` whose name ends with `Test`. Each method whose name starts with `test` is one test case. `Test(HelloTestSetup)` names the Setup that the test uses. The Setup file must be in the same folder as the test.

`this.construct(CounterService)` makes the service in the same way that Tachyon makes it for the page. `Fake` marks the field `greetingClient`, and `construct` gives the fake to the service in place of the real `GreetingClient`. So the test does not call the server. A controller is made in the same way: `this.construct(GreetingController)` makes the controller, and the test calls `getGreeting` directly, without HTTP. `GreetingClient` needs no test, because Tachyon writes its method. The Ruby controller test also uses `construct`. Where a tab does not use `construct`, the test makes the class itself, such as `GreetingController()` in Python, because the class needs nothing from Tachyon. Dart uses `construct<CounterService>(CounterService)` with a typed `Fake` field. Its generated `GreetingClient` is bound to this test’s BehaviorContext, and HelloTestSetup supplies a fake HTTP adapter returning the typed greeting data. The awaited `askServer` case exercises the service and its generated client decoder without a network request. Each service keeps the fake passed at construction; changing the test field does not replace an existing service’s dependency.

C# uses `construct<CounterService>()` with a typed `Fake` field. Each test creates its own BehaviorSignal and BehaviorContext, then passes that context to the generated `GreetingClient` constructor. `HelloTestSetup` explicitly constructs the stateless `GreetingFakeDelegate` adapter and returns the typed greeting data through the existing adapter boundary. The service captures its client when constructed. The three cases check increment, typed message decoding, and independent captured contexts: disposing the first context refuses its later call with `CANCELLED`, while the second service still succeeds. Changing or clearing the Fake field does not replace either existing service’s client. The delegate stays in `client/delegates`, and the TestSetup stays beside the test in `client/tests`.

F# uses `this.construct<CounterService>()` with a typed `Fake` property, `[<Fake>]` above `member val GreetingClient : GreetingClient = Unchecked.defaultof<GreetingClient> with get, set`. `construct` sets the `Needs` properties of the service from the Fake properties with the same name and type. While the Fake property is empty, the service gets a `GreetingClient` bound to this test's BehaviorContext, so the adapter of `HelloTestSetup` answers with the greeting and no request leaves the test. `HelloTestSetup` constructs the stateless `GreetingFakeDelegate` adapter itself; the delegate stays in `client/delegates`, and the production build leaves it out because only the TestSetup uses it. The third case gives each service its own client: `GreetingClient(firstContext)` uses a context that the test creates and owns. Disposing that context refuses the next call of the first service with `CANCELLED`, while the second service still succeeds. Changing or clearing the Fake property does not replace the client of a service that already exists. The private method `RefusalOf` catches the `BehaviorError`, because a test case only asserts.

Rust uses a `Fake` field `greeting_client: std::cell::RefCell<Option<std::sync::Arc<GreetingClient>>>` and `let mut counter: CounterService = self.construct();`. `construct` calls the constructor that Tachyon writes for the `Needs` fields. While the Fake field is empty, it gives the service a `GreetingClient` that uses this test's BehaviorContext, so the adapter of `HelloTestSetup` answers with the typed greeting and no request leaves the test. To give the service another client, put it in the field first. A test case can be an `async fn`; Tachyon runs it to the end, and `counter.ask_server().await` then saves the message.

Go uses a `// @Fake` field `greetingClient *GreetingClient` and `test.construct(counter)`, which fills the `Needs` fields of the service. While the Fake field is empty, the service gets a `GreetingClient` that uses this test's BehaviorContext, so `HelloTestSetup` answers through its `Exchange` method and no request leaves the test. To give the service another client, set the field first.

Kotlin uses a `Fake` field `var greetingClient: GreetingClient? = null` and `construct(CounterService::class)`, which calls the constructor that Tachyon writes for the `Needs` fields. While the Fake field is `null`, the service gets a `GreetingClient` that uses this test's BehaviorContext, so the adapter of `HelloTestSetup` answers with the greeting and no request leaves the test. To give the service another client, set the field first. A test case can be a `suspend fun`; Tachyon runs it to the end, so `counter.askServer()` has saved the message when the next line runs.

Java uses a `Fake` field `GreetingClient greetingClient = null;` and `construct(CounterService.class)`, which calls the constructor that Tachyon writes for the `Needs` fields. While the Fake field is `null`, the service gets a `GreetingClient` that uses this test's BehaviorContext, so the adapter of `HelloTestSetup` answers with the greeting and no request leaves the test. To give the service another client, set the field first. Test units run on the JVM, which has no browser transport: a client without an adapter fails with the code `http-adapter`.

Ruby uses a `Fake` field, `#[Fake]` above `attr_accessor :greeting_client`, and `construct(CounterService)`. While the Fake field is `nil`, the service gets a `GreetingClient` that uses this test's BehaviorContext, so the adapter of `HelloTestSetup` answers with the greeting and no request leaves the test. To give the service another client, set the field first, for example with `self.greeting_client = ...`. Test units run in CRuby, which has no browser transport: a client without an adapter fails with `Required behavior adapter is missing.`

Python test units have no `construct`. In a test unit, Tachyon gives the service a constructor that takes its `Needs` fields in order, so the test passes the client itself: `CounterService(self.greeting_client)`. The field `greeting_client: Annotated[GreetingClient, fake]` is the Fake: it is `None` at the start of each case. The second case makes a `GreetingClient` and sets its `behaviors` to `self.behaviors`, the context of `HelloTestSetup`, so the adapter of `HelloTestSetup` answers with the greeting and no request leaves the test. Its `exchange` method returns a dict, and the client reads it into the `Greeting` dataclass as on the page. A test case can be an `async def`; Tachyon runs it to the end, so `await counter.ask_server()` has saved the message when the next line runs.

Lua uses a `Fake` field, `-- @Fake` and `---@type GreetingClient` above `greeting_client = nil`, and `self:construct(CounterService)`. While the Fake field is `nil`, the service gets a `GreetingClient` that uses this test's BehaviorContext, so `HelloTestSetup` answers through its `exchange` method and no request leaves the test. To give the service another client, set the field first. Test units run in the `lua` interpreter, which has no browser transport: a client without an adapter fails with the code `HTTP_REQUEST`.

Swift uses a `Fake` field `var greetingClient: GreetingClient? = nil` and `let counter: CounterService = try construct()`, which calls the initializer that Tachyon writes for the `Needs` fields. While the Fake field is `nil`, the service gets a `GreetingClient` that uses this test's BehaviorContext, so the adapter of `HelloTestSetup` answers with the greeting and no request leaves the test. To give the service another client, set the field first. A test case is an `async throws` method, so `try await counter.askServer()` has saved the message when the next line runs.

C++ uses a `Fake` field `[[Fake]] GreetingClient greetingClient;` and `CounterService counter = construct<CounterService>();`. `construct` makes the service the way the page makes it, and every `Needs` field of the Fake's type gets the Fake field's object instead of the shared one. `HelloTestSetup` has a static `configure()` method that returns `BehaviorAdapters`. `adapters.http["greeting"]` answers each request of `GreetingClient` (the adapter name is the client name without `Client`), here with the typed `Greeting`, so no request leaves the test. A request with no answer fails its case with the code `HTTP_ADAPTER`. A test case can return `Task<void>`; Tachyon runs it to the end, so `co_await counter.askServer();` has saved the message when the next line runs. C++ test units compile with clang++ and run as a native binary. The server test is a C++ test unit too: `GreetingController controller = construct<GreetingController>();` makes the controller, and the test calls `getGreeting()` directly, without HTTP. `GreetingTestSetup` is a class marked `[[TestSetup]]`, and its static `configure` method returns empty `BehaviorAdapters`, because the controller needs nothing from outside. `ty test` compiles the server test with clang++, like a C++ controller, and runs it once; Emscripten is not needed.

Run `ty test` in the project folder. Then stop `ty preview` (press Ctrl+C) and run `ty preview` again. It starts, because a test case now calls every public method. A test must really call a method: a call on the fake `greetingClient` does not count for `GreetingClient`, and writing only the name of a method does not count at all. `ty test --coverage` shows which case first called each method.

Result: `ty test` prints one ok line for each test case and ends with 0 failed.
